extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, petitioners, patent owners, and USPTO staff involved in inter partes review, post-grant review, and covered business method patent review
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural rules and substantive thresholds for instituting and conducting inter partes review, post-grant review, and covered business method patent review under the AIA, including scheduling, joinder, supplemental evidence, standing, and burdens of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for substitute claims / motion to amend authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorization to file an additional motion to amend may be denied where the patent owner 'facially cannot meet one of the requirements (e.g., no support for the new claims)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denying authorization where the patent owner lacks support for new claims increases efficiency and prevents unnecessary opposition briefing and Board decision-writing. The Board will evaluate whether the patent owner meets the requirements for proposed substitute claims before authorizing filing of a motion to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling order timing — one year completion and default deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent with the decision to institute the review, the Board will enter a Scheduling Order that sets due dates taking into account complexity but ensuring the trial is completed within one year of institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The default Scheduling Order generally provides the petitioner with three months for discovery and for filing a petitioner’s reply to the patent owner’s response and any opposition to the motion to amend. Parties may request adjustments to the Scheduling Order at the initial conference call; the Scheduling Order may be modified by stipulation or authorized motion, subject to the Office’s ability to complete the review timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner’s right to present new evidence in opposition to an amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 42.23 provides for oppositions and replies; a petitioner will be afforded an opportunity to respond fully to an amendment and may supplement evidence submitted with their petition to respond to new issues arising from proposed substitute claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No authorization is needed to file an opposition to an amendment. Petitioners may submit new expert declarations directed to proposed substitute claims. Oppositions and replies must comply with content requirements for motions; a reply may only respond to arguments raised in the corresponding opposition. Per the Practice Guide, a reply that raises a new issue or belatedly presents evidence will not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation counts each instituted proceeding separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Where multiple instituted proceedings are consolidated, each proceeding is counted towards any limit that might be established because each is a separately instituted proceeding that is thereafter consolidated into a single proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation does not reduce the count of instituted proceedings for statutory or programmatic limits; practitioners should treat each instituted review as separately counted even if consolidated later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder — timing and factors for granting
rubrics_metrics.description: Joinder may be requested by filing a motion within one month of the date that the trial is instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether to grant joinder, the Office will consider particular facts including how consolidation impacts the Office’s ability to complete reviews timely (e.g., impact on Scheduling Order). The Director may adjust time periods for managing more complex consolidated cases. A request for joinder filed after the one-month period must meet the standards set forth in the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: No party 'replacement' under AIA; effect of settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA does not provide for the 'replacement' of a party. A petitioner may settle with the patent owner and upon entering the joint request, the review will terminate with respect to the petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties cannot rely on a statutory mechanism to replace a consenting petitioner; settlement terminates that petitioner’s participation under 35 U.S.C. 317 and 327.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stays, transfers, consolidation or termination are fact-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the rules, a stay, transfer, consolidation or termination would be an option; whether ordered and the order of resolution depends on particular facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will consider the impact on each proceeding case-by-case. A stay (suspending time for taking actions) is expected to be rare. In considering a stay, the goal of completing the proceeding in a timely manner will be taken into account. Relevant statutory references include 35 U.S.C. 315(d), 325(d), 316(a)(11), and 326(a)(11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information — one-month deadline and standards for later requests
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may seek authorization to file supplemental information relevant to a claim for which the trial has been instituted within one month of the date the trial is instituted. Any request not made within one month must show why the information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration would be in the interests-of-justice (§§ 42.123(b) and 42.223(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the submission is not relevant to a claim for which the trial has been instituted, the party must show both that the information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier and that consideration would be in the interests-of-justice (§§ 42.123(c) and 42.223(c)). These rules implement 35 U.S.C. 316(a)(3) and 326(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion when supplemental information is allowed — additional discovery and motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board grants a motion to file late supplemental information, the Board may authorize the patent owner to take additional discovery or to file a motion to amend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining whether to authorize an additional motion to amend, the Board will consider whether a petitioner has submitted supplemental information after the time period set for filing a motion to amend in §42.121(a) or §42.221(a). The Board may also extend the time period for completing the review. The Board may consider whether a late submission represents an improper use of the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for misconduct and improper delay
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may impose a sanction against a party for misconduct, including any action that harasses or causes unnecessary delay or cost (§42.12(a)(7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to set forth their best grounds and supporting evidence in the petition to avoid sanctions and the risk of denial under §42.108(b). The Board may consider sanctions or refuse to consider late or improper submissions that cause delay or unnecessary cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization to raise new grounds of unpatentability from supplemental evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a party is authorized to raise new grounds of unpatentability based upon supplemental information will be determined on a case-by-case basis taking into account the particular facts surrounding the supplemental information submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While supplemental evidence may be relevant to a new ground, the party must additionally show that consideration of the supplemental evidence would be in the interests-of-justice. If a new ground is authorized, estoppel may apply (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel for grounds raised or reasonably could have been raised
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel applies for any ground that the petition raised or reasonably could have raised during the review (35 U.S.C. 315(e) and 325(e)); estoppel would apply where a new ground is authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should be cognizant that authorization to raise new grounds based on later evidence can create estoppel effects; this influences the strategic decision whether to seek authorization for new grounds and what evidence to include in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Guide scheduling order is a guideline; parties may propose dates and stipulate modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheduling order in the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide is a general guideline based on the rules. Parties are encouraged to recommend particular dates within the general framework that work for both prior to the initial conference call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may stipulate to modify most deadlines set within the scheduling order; any further modification must be by authorized motion (§42.20(b)). Whether such a motion is authorized or granted depends on the particular circumstances of the case including the Office’s ability to complete the review in a timely manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM 'charged with infringement' standard for standing
rubrics_metrics.description: For covered business method patent review, 'charged with infringement' means a real and substantial controversy regarding infringement of a covered business method patent such that the petitioner would have standing to bring a declaratory judgment action in Federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will provide more guidance by providing a rule that sets forth the standard for 'charged with infringement' in a revision to the Office Patent Trial Practice Guide. Mere discussions about licensing do not necessarily constitute a charge of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner’s burden for CBM eligibility and technological invention exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 42.304(a) requires that the petitioner demonstrate that the patent for which review is sought is a covered business method patent, including demonstrating that the patent is not for a technological invention; the showing for both covered business method patent and technological invention is based on what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office adopts a 'demonstrate' standard (rather than mere prima facie showing or simple certification). The petitioner bears the burden to show at least one claim is not directed to a technological invention to establish standing under §42.302.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of standing and timing to challenge standing
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition is required to show specifically that it meets the requirements of §42.302 (i.e., that the petitioner, the petitioner’s real party-in-interest, or a privy of the petitioner has been sued for infringement or has been charged with infringement). A showing can only be made through sufficient proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facially improper standing is a basis for denying the petition without proceeding to the merits. A patent owner should challenge standing no later than the filing of the patent owner preliminary response (§42.207(a)). The petitioner must, at a minimum, certify with explanation that the patent is a covered business method patent and that the petitioner meets the eligibility requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM nexus requirement to financial product or service
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the rules, the petitioner must demonstrate that the patent for which review is sought is a covered business method patent — i.e., that the patent claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operation used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, and which is not a technological invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration is claim-based. The rules do not limit which claims may be challenged to only those directed specifically to the covered business method; petitioner should articulate how the claims satisfy the statutory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement to present best grounds and evidence in petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners are encouraged to set forth their best grounds of unpatentability and supporting evidence in their petitions, lest the petitioner risk a determination by the Board not to institute the review or deny the asserted grounds of unpatentability (§42.108(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on supplemental information obtained later carries risk: late submissions may be denied, may require showing in interests-of-justice, may lead to sanctions, or may affect Board authorization to amend or timing of the review.
